The ES is a
Guideline for Agency workers and is not meant to replace sound clinical child
welfare judgment in decision-making.…

…These more severe
cases (referencing adult conflict) will require an investigation of whether the
child appears to be showing behaviours indicative of the emotional or
psychological harm.…

…Workers need to
ask: Is this a case of an affinity with one parent, divorce-specific alignment,
justified rejection due to intimate partner violence or maltreatment (justified
rejection), an unjustified rejection (alienation) or a mixed case?…

…The agency may also
be concerned that the parents are using them to advance concerns about the
other parent, either for family litigation purposes or for other clinical
reasons.…

Like all legal and
mental health professionals, CPAs are challenged by cases where there are high
levels of adult or parental conflict and when one parent is seriously
undermining the child’s relationship with the other parent.…

(In referencing
severe cases, the authors note:) …The psychologically abusive conduct and
intrusive parenting of the alienating parent is often related to personality
disorders or even mental illness. There is severe and frequent denigration,
bad-mouthing and interference with the child’s contact with the rejected
parent. Favoured parents usually characterize any blocking of the child’s time
with the other parent as protection, despite repeated investigations or
evidence that demonstrates that there is no risk of future harm or that it is
highly improbable, or as vindication of their child’s “right” to not have a
relationship with the other parent.

Children in severe
cases exhibit to a significant degree all eight of the behaviours identified by
Gardner as markers of alienation. Temper tantrums, panic attacks or phobic
reactions may occur. Generally, children will be more rigid and extreme in
their reactions to the rejected parent, despite a history of positive
interactions. Children and their alienating parents may share paranoid
fantasies, sometimes accompanied by an “us vs them” presentation applied to
others such as assessors, teachers or therapists, not only the rejected
parent.…

Once their children
are severely alienated, alienating parents may suggest or even tell their child
to see the other parent, knowing that the child will refuse.
Often,
alienating parents will state that they will not or cannot “force” the child to
have contact, while noting that the child has a “right” to make up their own
mind about choosing to have or not to have contact, in effect severing ties,
with the other parent…

The longer
alienation lasts, the harder it is to remedy.

[
955
]

In section 10 of their guide (pages 118 to 154),
the authors discuss coordinated interdisciplinary interventions. When
discussing reunification of a child with an absent parent, the authors suggest
that:

Two critical
questions need to be asked:

1)

Irrespective of the nature and severity of the
parent-child contact problem, is it in the child’s best interests to either
develop or repair a relationship with the resisted parent and to modify the
child’s relationship with the favoured parent?

2)

Can improvements to the parent-child contact
problem be realistically achieved given the family circumstances, the
characteristics of the parents and the resources available in the community?
(Page 119)

[
956
]

While discussing mild and some moderate cases,
the authors note:

…While a brief
acquiescence to a child to not require contact is reasonable in most
situations, a prolonged period of “give it some time” is not advised, precisely
because it is often difficult for legal and mental health and child protection
professionals to predict whether affinities or alignments will develop into
alienation or justified rejection…. (Page 120)

Unlike traditional
therapy, in high conflict cases where personality disorders and noncompliance
with authority are common, court directed counselling should have only limited
confidentiality (Greenberg, Doi Fick & Schneider, 2012; Sullivan & Kelly
2001)
Parents need to be accountable, and the court needs to monitor the
family and enforce orders as required and in the best interests of the child….
(Page 128)

The court order or
agreement needs to articulate the intervention goals (Fidler, Bala and Saini,
2013). (Page 130)

Often, weekly
therapy aimed at addressing alienation is intensive and requires at least 6 to
9 months to complete, and in some cases, as long as 2 years. However, if there
is (sic) there has been little or no change in the behaviour of the child or
favoured parent within 3 months, there will be real concerns about whether
therapy is an effective intervention…. (Page 131)

In some parent-child
contact problem cases, supervised visitation (also called supervised access or
contact) or supervised exchanges from one parent to the other for unsupervised
contact may be indicated initially, to protect against the possibility of adult
conflict or abuse to maintain the child’s contact with the parent, while
allowing time to investigate the varied and often conflicting allegations.
While supervised access is not therapy per se, it may provide a measure of
safety and security for parents and an opportunity to build trust.… Caution
should be used in having family members supervise as they may not be
sufficiently objective or neutral. (Pages 131 – 132)

Case management by
one judge is important with high conflict parents. (Page 134)

A judicial “push”
toward therapy may have positive effects, though there are limits to what can
be accomplished in therapy when a parent or child is unwilling to participate
or unmotivated to change. Counselling is most likely to be effective when a
judge persuades parents of its value and the importance of the child having a
positive relationship with both parents…  However, counselling may be
ineffective if the parties are highly resistant to intervention and are only
attending to avoid a finding of contempt of court. (Page 135)

When the favoured
parent’s views are inflexible and there is little insight or willingness to
change, a warning about a possible reversal of custody, a supervision order, or
placement of the child with a third party in the event of noncompliance with
contact or treatment orders may be an important change-agent. (Page 135)

Often, but not
always, the more time a child spends with a resisted parent, the greater
likelihood for their relationship to be strengthened. Extended periods of
contact with the resisted parent over holidays, such as during summer or
Christmas vacation, coupled with restricted contact with the favoured parent
may be helpful to repair the strained relationship and prevent further
deterioration in the relationship. (Page 136)

In alienation cases,
any opportunity for the favoured, often custodial, parent to control the
parenting time schedule may be exploited. ( Page 136)

The failure of the
court to enforce orders only serves to reinforce a parent’s narcissism, false
sense of control or power and their disregard for authority. A range of
sanctions can be imposed for contempt under rule 31(5) of the Family Law Rules.
(Page 138)

In severe and some
moderate cases, education or therapy alone, in the absence of a temporary
interruption in contact with the favoured parent, is unlikely to reverse the
alienation.… (Page 143)

One option to consider
when less intrusive legal or clinical remedies have failed and the rejected
parent can adequately care for the child, is a change of custody. A custody
reversal may be warranted when the rejected parent demonstrates more
sensitivity to and understanding of the child’s psychological needs than the
favoured parent. To prevent the child to reestablish the previously loving
relationship with the rejected parent, the changing custody is likely to
require a temporary suspension of, or supervised contact with the alienating
parent, and may require therapeutic support. (Page 143)

It is important to
recognize that there is no perfect parent-child relationship. Rather a healthy
and functional relationship will include the child’s ability to accept and
integrate both good and bad qualities of the parent, coupled with flexible
thinking, the capacity for multiple perspective taking, good communication and
problem solving skills, and so on, all of which are indices of mature
interpersonal skills and relationships. (Page 144)

In other cases, it
is expected that the child will “vote with his feet,” regardless of what order
is made. In some cases, the judge might also consider it appropriate to meet
with the child or write the child a letter (copying the parents and lawyers
involved in the case) to explain the decision. (Pages 144 - 145)

For some, custody
reversal is considered a punitive action against a well-intentioned and
protective, albeit misguided, parent. Others maintain that placing the child
with the rejected parent, when appropriate, is not a punitive measure, but
rather one to protect a child from the unrelenting emotional abuse by the
alienating parent, even when the favoured parent is not conscious of their own
attempts to turn the child against other parent. (Page 146)

In severe cases,
through a process of emotional exploitation, indoctrination, manipulation and
intrusive parenting, the child has developed a distorted view of reality. False
beliefs, irrational fears, and anxieties have been instilled and promoted; like
a prejudice,
the child has been taught to hate.
The child may truly
believe that the rejected parent is unsafe, abusive or unworthy, or the child
may know this is not the case but persist in their rejection. Either way, the
child is being emotionally harmed or at risk of significant emotional harm.
(Page 147)

Consequently,
proponents of custody reversal for the most severe cases observe that there are
also ethical issues in not intervening to protect children from alienating
abusive parenting (Warshak, 2010a). It is argued that we have a legal and moral
obligation to protect children from psychological or emotional abuse, and
further, that the prevention of abuse must take priority over the goal of
attempting to have the child spend more time with the rejected parent. We must
consider the risks of doing nothing, which in fact is doing something. (Page
147)

While some children
may experience difficulties in the short term with the transition from the
favoured to the rejected parent, in other cases, despite their prior assertions
to the contrary and much to the surprise of many of the adults and
professionals involved, children transition easily. Once out of the orbit of
the favoured parent, an alienated child can transform very well, sometimes very
quickly, from staunchly resisting the rejected parent, to being able to show
and receive love from that parent. The child, now removed from the role of the
decision-maker, may feel liberated to resume what was a positive relationship
with the parent they have not been free to love in the presence of the favoured
parent. (Page 148)

Amy Baker’s research
(2007) (supported by that of Clawar & Rivlin, 1991), indicates that
retrospectively, many of the adults recall as children secretly wishing that
someone “call their bluff” and insist they have a relationship with the parent
they claimed to fear or hate. (Page 148)

The ultimate goal is
for the child to have a healthy relationship with
both
parents. However,
in more severe alienation cases, the child’s relationship with the rejected
parent cannot be repaired, normalized or strengthened as long as there is
intermittent contact with the alienating parent that involves controlling,
intrusive and manipulative interference. Once the relationship with the
rejected parent is repaired, consideration can be given to reintegrating the
favoured parent back into child’s life. Criteria for resuming this contact
include the favoured parent’s participation in educational programs and therapy

and
the demonstration of behavioural change. The therapist reports back
to court, which then determines the parenting time schedule for the child and
the previously alienating parent. Initially, contact may require supervision
and ongoing monitoring by the court, with a view to normalizing the child’s
contact with both parents. (Pages 149 - 150)

In severe cases,
including those whose previous therapy has not been effective, a program such
as “
Family Bridges: A Workshop for Troubled and Alienated Parent-Child
Relationships
” (Family Bridges) may assist the child(ren) and rejected
parent to make the transition
after
the court determines that an interim
or permanent change in custody to the rejected parent is in the child’s best
interest (Rand & Warshak, 2008; Warshak, 2010a). The change in custody
provides the rejected parent with the legal authority to make health care
decisions for the child. In addition, an order for a temporary interruption in
contact with the favoured parent usually at least for 3 months, is necessary to
allow for the reintegration with the rejected parent to take effect and
solidify. The workshop is run by two professionals at a time, can occur in
Ontario or in the United States (often Texas or California) and last between 4
and 5 days. (Page 150)

acknowledgement of desire for reconciliation

962
]

In the same table, the following behaviours are
noted with respect to typical behaviours exhibited by the favoured (alienating)
parent (at pages 84 - 85):

•

No encouragement of calls by child to the other
parent between contacts; rationalizes that child does not ask

•

Indulges child with material possessions and
privileges

•

Sets few limits or is rigid about routines, rules,

•

No concern for missed time with other parent

Rejected parent is discouraged or refused

•

Doesn’t

Portrays other parent as dangerous…

Exaggerates negative attributes of other parent

Projection of own thoughts, feelings, and

Does not correct child’s rude, defiant and/or

Convinced of harm, when there is no evidence

[

This court finds that while all of these tables
and indicia are helpful, “one” in this book is more poignant than any other. On
page 78, the authors state the following:

Toronto lawyer
Philip Epstein, during an interview on August 15, 2010 while commenting on
parental alienation), for example stated, “It’s like obscenity, you know it
when you see it.”

[
964
]

This court in no way professes to have
specialized knowledge of what is parental alienation.

[
965
]

This court acknowledges that there was no expert
evidence given with respect to whether or not the actions of the respondent in
this particular case constituted parental alienation.

[
966
]

The reason is that this court found that it
would not be appropriate to have Howard Hurwitz give evidence as to whether or
not he believed there was parental alienation in this case based on information
that he had received from the applicant mother recently.

]

The court’s rationale of course was that while
Mr. Hurwitz had done an assessment, he had not had an opportunity to update
that assessment and had not seen the children since his assessment was

assessment was completed.

court may make a determination as to whether or not parental alienation has

[

]

This court totally agrees with Mr. Epstein’s
(regarding parental alienation) analysis that, especially in severe cases such
as this, “you know it when you see it.”

Variation

17

IV.  Analysis

…

A)  The Threshold
Condition: Material

Change

10        Before the
court can consider the merits of the application for variation, it must be satisfied
there has been a material change in the circumstances of the child since the
last custody order was made. Section 17(5) provides that the court shall not
vary a custody or access order absent a change in the “condition, means, needs
or other circumstances of the child”. Accordingly, if the applicant is unable
to show the existence of a material change, the inquiry can go no farther:
Wilson
v. Grassick
(1994),
1994 CanLII 4709 (SK CA)
, 2 R.F.L. (4
th
) 291 (Sask.

C.A.).

13        It follows
that before entering on the merits of an application to vary a custody order
the judge must be satisfied of: (1) a change in the condition, means, needs or
circumstances of the child and/or the ability of the parents to meet the needs
of the child; (2) which materially affects the child; and (3) which was either
not foreseen or could not have been reasonably contemplated  by the judge who
made the initial

order.

[
979
]

The Wildman J. order flows from the Corkery J.
order and therefore, this court will deal with the Corkery J. order first.
Essentially, the Wildman J. order is the financial support order that arises
out of the parenting order being the Corkery J. order.

[
980
]

This court could simply find that since both
parties are seeking to change the Corkery J. order and both are alleging there
has been a material change in circumstances on which to base that change that
nothing further need be said on that point.

[
981
]

However, independent of the positions taken by
the parties, this court finds that there is overwhelming evidence that there
has been a material change in circumstances affecting these children.

[
982
]

At the time that the consent order was entered
into, there was a great deal of effort spent in outlining with great
specificity the parenting time with each parent and the respective rights and
obligations of each parent relating to elements of custody. Essentially, as
noted earlier, the consent order was an adoption of the recommendations made by
Howard Hurwitz in the parenting plan attached to his section 30 custody access
assessment.

[
983
]

That order resulted in a parallel parenting
regime and resulted in the children spending roughly equal amounts of time with
each parent.

[
984
]

If the parents can agree on anything at this
point in time, it is that the current order is not functioning. Each has of
course a different perspective on why that is occurring and each has a
different perspective on what the solution should be.

[
985
]

Given the children’s resistance to spending time
with their mother and given the need for police enforcement to create a
situation pursuant to which the children do spend time with their mother, this
court finds that there is without question a material change in circumstances
from that which existed at the time of the Corkery J. order.

[
986
]

In addition, the current situation could not
have been anticipated at that time, even though there were signs of what was to
come virtually immediately after that order was entered into.

[
987
]

Having found that there has been a material
change in circumstances, the court must next look at the “second prong” of the
relevant paragraphs of the
Divorce Act
and as outlined in
Gordon v. Goertz
.

[
988
]

That next “step” is outlined in paragraphs 18
and 19 of
Gordon v. Goertz
[6]

as follows:

B)
The Best Interests of the Child

…

same

principle

holds

true

when

an

applicant

is

able

to

demonstrate

a

material

change

in

circumstances

in

a

custodial variation proceeding. In order
to determine the child's best interest, the judge must consider how the change
impacts on all aspects of the child's life. To put it another way, the material
change places the original order in question; all factors relevant to that

circumstances.

19.       What
principles should

guide

the

judge

on

this

fresh

review

of

the

situation?

This

inquiry takes

us

to
the

last

clause of

s.

17(5)

of

the

Divorce
Act
:”

…

in making the
variation order, the court shall take into consideration only the best
interests  of the child as determined by reference to that change". The
amendments to the
Divorce Act

in 1986 (S.C. 1986, c. 4 (now R.S.C. 1985,
c. 3 (2nd Supp.)) elevated the best interests of the child from a
"paramount" consideration, to the
"only"
relevant

issue.

[
989
]

As detailed elsewhere in this decision, this
court has found that there has been severe parental alienation by the
respondent father which has resulted in the children taking the actions that
they have and taking the “position” that they no longer wish to have regular

[
990
]

The court now wishes to make reference to other
cases cited by the respondent.

Collison v Neely
[7]

[
991
]

This case involved a 14-year-old daughter who
did not want to return to her mother’s. Presumably the respondent made

fait accompli”.

[
992
]

The only similarity between that case and the
case with which we are dealing is that it is a 14-year-old child who does not

993

The case is distinguishable as it involves a

is decided under the

not the

.

Further, it is a case of the Ontario Court of
Justice and therefore obviously this court is not bound by that decision.

Mikkelsen and Mikkelsen
[8]

[
995
]

This case was decided by Justice Gordon of the
Ontario Superior Court of Justice. The children were aged 16, 14 and 11 at the
time of the application. In that case they did not want to see their father.

[
996
]

The main distinguishing factor between that case
and the present one was that in that case there were two separate professional
assessments which found that the children’s views and preferences possessed

[
997
]

This case is totally distinguishable from that
case given that this court finds that the children’s opinions are far from

]

The court in that case found, as does this

Supple v Cashman
[9]

[
999
]

This is a case decided by Justice Sheffield of
the Ontario Court of Justice. Although this case is certainly not binding on

this court.

[
1000
]

In that

case, the children were 14 and 12. They were refusing

[

]

This court wishes to quote the following paragraphs from that
decision namely,

Evidence and
Positions of the Parties

….

8
I have read the report of Dr. Worenklein, which
is filed as part of the trial record, and have heard his oral testimony. Dr.
Worenklein was qualified as an expert in child psychology with particular
expertise in the area of "parental alienation". It was made clear to
the court, at the outset of Dr. Worenklein's testimony, that both he and the
father's legal counsel, Mr. Brian Ludmer, had served together on a committee
which had, as its principle purpose, a declaration that the issue of parental
alienation be recognized as a medical diagnosis under the DSM-V. This request
was unsuccessful.

9
I found Dr. Worenklein to be a helpful witness.
He expressed the opinion that Ms.
Supple
was
alienating her children from their father. He based this opinion on his
observations of the boys, of their expressed wishes, and of their interactions
with either parent. Dr. Worenklein noted that, although the boys expressed in
very clear terms that they did not wish to see their father, they were warm and
loving with their father while participating in a one and a half hour interview
and observation session with Mr.
Cashman
. He
saw no evidence in the children's interactions with their father that suggested
that they either feared him or wanted to end their contact with him. Following
this session, Dr. Worenklein saw no indication that Nathan was either homicidal
or suicidal. According to Dr. Worenklein, "actions speak louder than
words". The expert opined that it is a sign of parental alienation where
children express a desire to end all contact with one parent, but show clear
affection towards that parent when alone with him or her. Dr. Worenklein
concluded that the best course of action for the children would be to place
them in the sole custody of their father while their mother attends specialized
therapy to end her alienating behaviours. Only once Ms.
Supple
had demonstrated that she would not engage in alienating
behaviours would contact between her and her boys resume.

10
Not surprisingly, Ms.
Supple

took strong exception to these recommendations. She suggested that Dr.
Worenklein was biased. She argued that she had done all that she could to
foster the boys' relationship with their father and that she has not engaged in
alienating behaviour. In her view, the boys' relationship with their father has
deteriorated because of the father's own actions and because of his rigid,
controlling nature. For instance, the Court heard ample evidence that the
children's father and paternal grandfather take issue with the children's
decisions regarding such things as hairstyles and shoe sizes. While the father
and paternal grandfather deny that they have made disparaging remarks with
respect to Trevor's long hair and possible sexual orientation, I do not accept
their evidence on this point. Additionally, the father has repeatedly failed to
return the children to their mother's home in a timely fashion, which further
exacerbates the children's stress when they are with him.

…

Analysis

Custody and
Access

…

18
In my view, having reviewed all of the evidence,
this is not a clear case of extreme parental alienation. Rather, in this case,
I find that there are elements of alienation and elements of realistic, or
justified, estrangement. With respect to signs of alienation, I note that Ms.
Supple
is very emotionally attached to her
children, and her children to her. The level of attachment of these adolescent
boys to their mother is somewhat unusual. For instance, Trevor continues to
crawl into bed with his mother on occasion. Additionally, the boys dislike
attending sleepovers because they do not wish to leave their mother alone. It
is clear to me that there is some blurring of the line between parent and
child, in the sense that the boys feel the need to protect their mother, which
is not a role that a child should be pressured to fill. It is also very evident
to me that the children are highly involved in the conflict between their
parents and that they feel the stress of trying to resolve this conflict.
Again, this is inappropriate, although I do not believe that the blame falls
entirely on the mother's shoulders. Rather, both parties have inappropriately
involved the boys in their conflict and the boys have been privy to far too
much information about the legal issues. Finally, I find that Ms.
Supple
has made numerous unfounded allegations of
abuse — both towards herself and her children — against Mr.
Cashman
.

19
On the other hand, I also see evidence that the
children are justified in their desire to limit their interactions with their
father. I accept evidence that the children's father and paternal grandfather
and step-grandmother are overbearing and controlling of the boys. It is very
clear to me that Mr.
Cashman
genuinely loves
his children and cares about their wellbeing. However, I find that some of Ms.
Supple's
allegations of emotional abuse have
merit; specifically, I find that Mr.
Cashman

and his father have ridiculed and scrutinized the boys over their hair and
dress style choices. I also find that Mr.
Cashman

has very rigid beliefs concerning the types of activities in which his boys
should be involved, beliefs which are at odds with the children's desires.
While the children acknowledge that they love their father, the constant
pressure to act and speak in a manner which is consistent with their father's
traditional views of gender roles is certain to be stressful for a child who is
seeking to express himself in a way that conflicts with those roles. It is
clear to me that each of these parents has a distinctive approach to parenting.
It is when those approaches conflict that the children are forced to make
choices. On this point I am sensitive to the opinion of Dr. Worenklein who
opined that children should be allowed to make some choices but that there are
others they should not have to make. In this regard I find that Ms.
Supple
generally strikes a better balance.

[
1002
]

In that particular case, the court did not accept the recommendation
of Dr. Worenklein.

[
1003
]

The court did however note that the expert opined that a sign of
parental alienation was where children express a desire to end all contact with
one parent but show clear affection towards that parent when left alone with
him or her. This is a situation similar to what this court has heard in that
when the children are alone with their mother for periods of time, they do have
a “normal” relationship.

[
1004
]

In the
Supple
case, the court decided not to follow the
recommendation of the expert and found that in that particular case it was not
a clear case of extreme parental alienation but rather contained elements of
realistic, or justified in estrangement.

[
1005
]

In that particular case, the court found that there was evidence
that the children’s father, paternal grandfather and step grandmother were
overbearing and controlling and that the mother’s allegations of emotional
abuse by the father and grandparents had merit.

[
1006
]

The court further found that the father had ridiculed and
scrutinized the boys over their hair and dress style choices. The father also
had very rigid beliefs concerning the types of activities in which the boys
should be involved which beliefs were at odds with the children’s desires.

[
1007
]

This court finds that the
Supple
case is totally
distinguishable from this case where none of those situations exist with the

Patterson v. Powell
[10]

[
1008
]

This case is a 2014 decision of Justice Pazaratz of the Ontario
Superior Court of Justice.

[
1009
]

The case deals with
the appropriateness of police enforcement of the Minutes of Settlement.

[
1010
]

Even though the parties consented to police having powers of
enforcement, the court found that this was not an appropriate remedy on a
long-term basis and that police enforcement of time with parents should be
limited in their use.

[
1011
]

In his decision, Justice Pazaratz said the following:

77
Increasingly, courts seem to recognize that —
especially when dealing with children — judges have an obligation to craft
comprehensive, holistic and durable court orders which have a likelihood of
success and compliance. High conflict files need to be identified and given
special attention. While disputes may inevitably arise, courts have a
responsibility to anticipate problems and build-in dispute resolution
mechanisms — rather than hand the mess over to police to sort it out.

78
If a judge anticipates future disputes or
non-compliance, the court may wish to remain seized of the matter, and
establish a framework to quickly deal with disputes — including contempt
proceedings — to ensure that the parties clearly understand expectations and
consequences.

79
In the absence of ongoing judicial intervention,
and serious consequences for disobedience of court orders, long-term police
enforcement clauses may prove to be both ineffectual and potentially
counter-productive. Non-compliant parents are unlikely to be influenced by
repeat police visits to their homes; but children are likely to be deeply (and
negatively) influenced.

[
1012
]

At paragraph 77 the court noted that “high conflict files need to be
identified and given special attention. While disputes may inevitably arise, courts have a responsibility
to anticipate problems and build-in dispute resolution mechanisms – rather than
hand the mess over to the police to sort it out.”

[
1013
]

This court concurs with the opinions of Justice Pazaratz and those
he quoted of Justice Quinn.

[
1014
]

This court does not see police enforcement as a long-term solution.
In this particular case, the children have expressed serious and understandable
frustration with police enforcement.

[
1015
]

It is for this very
reason that this court is ordering a therapeutic regime whereby this court is
attempting to deal with the root cause of the problem and not the symptom.

[
1016
]

This court would agree with the word picture of Justice Quinn that
where police enforcement of visitation between parents is necessary the parents have in fact failed.

[
1017
]

Contrary to the
position taken by the respondent, however this court finds that it is not the
mother who is failed as much as the father although she too has some degree of
ownership in the problem.

[
1018
]

This court is optimistic that the order imposed will result in a
dynamic which is totally different to that which the parties have experienced
since separation and that it will result in the children willingly spending quality time with each
parent rather than having to be “forced” to do so.

[
1019
]

Having said that, until there has been an opportunity for the
therapeutic intervention to change the attitudes of the respondent and the children, the provision for continued
police enforcement must remain in place to prevent the respondent from
thwarting the effectiveness of this court’s decision.

ARTICLES SUBMITTED BY THE
RESPONDENT

[
1020
]

In response to the evidence given by Howard Hurwitz with respect to
parental alienation, the court indicated to the respondent that articles on parental alienation could be
submitted on his behalf to be considered by the court. There were two such
articles submitted and the court will comment with respect to the same.

[
1021
]

Even though the respondent did not put forward any evidence to
qualify the authors of these two articles as “expert witnesses”, out of an
abundance of fairness to the respondent, this court has read and considered
these articles.

Alienated Children and Parental Separation: Legal Responses
in Canada’s Family Courts

[
1022
]

The respondent submitted this article authored by Nicholas Bala,
Barbara Jo Fidler, Dan Goldberg and Claire Houston being an article published
in the Queens Law Journal in 2007.

[
1023
]

This court found that the content of the article and the premises
contained therein were in accordance with the previous book entitled
Children
Who Resist Postseparation Parental Contact (A Different Approach for Legal and
Mental Health Professionals)
co-authored by Barbara Jo Fidler, Nicholas
Bala and Michael A. Saini.

[
1024
]

As well, there are a number of similarities between the premises set
out in this article and the book/guide co-authored by Barbara Jo Fidler,
Nicholas Bala and Howard Hurwitz. This is not surprising given that two of the
authors are co-authors of both.

[
1025
]

This court will, however, make reference to various paragraphs of
the article submitted by the respondent. Unfortunately, the pages are not
numbered and therefore the quotes will not be referenced by page number.

[
1026
]

As well, there are footnote references within the article. This
court did not see a need to cite all of the footnote references within the
article but those references may be found by reference to the article itself.

[
1027
]

The authors indicate the following:

Less adversarial approaches and therapeutic interventions are
appropriate for less severe cases, but in more severe cases, the threat of an
effective legal response is necessary.
Variation of custody is a drastic
response, but in more severe cases it may be the only way to stop emotionally
abusive alienating conduct
.

[
1028
]

This court agrees with that theory and having found that in this
particular case it is one of severe alienation, this court finds that a drastic
response is warranted in order to stop the emotionally abusive alienating
conduct.

[
1029
]

In discussing situations where, in a minority of cases, children
stridently reject one of the parents, the authors speak of unjustified
rejection versus “realistic estrangement”. The court agrees with the authors
that quite commonly both parents attempt to undermine the relationship with the
other parent. In this case, however, this court finds that the next quote from
this article is appropriate to this particular case.

In
some cases one parent alone should be seen as having responsibility for the
poor relationship between the other parent and child, ...

[
1030
]

The authors then go on to relate the history of parental alienation.
The history identified is very similar to that opined in the book co-authored
by Howard Hurwitz to which much reference has been made in this decision.
The
authors reference “parental alienation syndrome” (PAS) developed by American
psychiatrist Richard Gardner in the late 1980s
. The reference is as
follows:

It
was, however, only in the late 1980s that mental health and legal professionals
began to make significant use of the concept of “parental alienation.” This
occurred after an American psychiatrist, Richard Gardner, developed the concept
of “parental alienation syndrome” (PAS), defining it as:

a
disorder that arises primarily in the context of child-custody disputes. Its
primary manifestation is the child's campaign of denigration against a parent,
a campaign that has no justification. It results from the combination of a
programming (brainwashing) parent's indoctrinations and the child's own
contributions to the vilification of the target parent.
6

For
Gardner, the programming parent's primary motivation was to “gain leverage in
court” by encouraging the child to turn against “a good, loving parent.”
Conceptualizing one parent as “good,” and the other as the “programming”
parent, fits well with the adversarial model of a family justice system that
traditionally awarded custody to the “better” parent.

[
1031
]

As did Howard Hurwitz and his co-authors, these authors then
reference the concept that in the early 2000’s alienation was reformulated to
consider all family members and not just the alienating parent. Reference is
made to the work of American psychologists Joan Kelly and Janet Johnston. The
reference is that a child may “unreasonably” reject one parent despite the
absence of “alienating” conduct by the other parent. The court concurs that
this could, and in many cases does, occur.

[
1032
]

As with most cases, however, they are factually based; though in
this case, this court finds that this is not a situation where the children
have of their own accord “unreasonably” rejected their mother. The authors
reference this as follows:

In
the past decade, the concept of alienation has been reformulated in a more
sophisticated way that explicitly looks to the role of all family members in
the development of alienation. Instead of directing attention primarily at the
programming parent, American psychologists Joan Kelly and Janet Johnston
developed an approach that focuses on the alienated child:

one
who expresses freely, and persistently, unreasonable negative feelings and
beliefs (such as anger, hatred, rejection, and/or fear) toward a parent that
are significantly disproportionate to the child's actual experience with that
parent ... the problem of the alienated child begins with a primary focus on
the child, his or her observable behaviours, and parent-child relationships.

This
approach recognizes that a child may “unreasonably” reject one parent despite
the absence of “alienating” conduct by the other parent. Although empirical
research in this area is limited, one study by Johnston and her colleagues
suggests that while alienating conduct on the part of both parents is the norm
in high-conflict divorce cases, most children are actually resistant to
pressures from one parent to reject the other. Such a finding calls into
question the appropriateness of concentrating solely on the behaviour of one
parent to the detriment of all other possible causal factors. The
“systems-based model” proposed by Kelly and Johnston encourages clinicians to
consider a number of different factors when investigating possible cases of
alienation, including “the age and developmental level of the child, the
psychological vulnerability of the child, the behaviours and personalities of
both parents, sibling dynamics, the remarriage situation, and the adversarial

B. Judicial
Control of High Conflict Cases: Case Management, Detailed Orders and Costs

Contact
with a non-custodial parent should not be regarded as subject to the “wishes”
of the children
or the
convenience of a custodial parent. Absent concern about such issues as abuse,
which might result in a court order terminating access,
each parent should
be expected to support the children's relationship with the other parent, and
to take steps to ensure that the children have a positive attitude about that
relationship
.

A
significant portion of alienation cases involve parents who exhibit high levels
of conflict and who struggle to control each other through the legal process.
These parents often try to manipulate the legal process. Judicial case
management and detailed orders impose external controls with the objective of
disengaging the parents, reducing their conflict and ultimately improving the
emotional well-being of the children.

Case
management is the designation of one judge to deal with all motions and
applications before trial. Though it can be institutionally challenging to
arrange, it has clear value in high-conflict cases.
If a judge makes an
order after trial in an alienation case, it may be appropriate to make an order
to remain seized of the case to deal with possible review or enforcement
.
If only one judge remains involved with the case, he or she can better understand
the dynamics of the family dispute. Consequently,
this judge is less likely
to be manipulated and more likely to provide consistency, predictability and
stability. The parents are more likely to comply with the exhortations of
“their” judge who they expect will address violations of court orders
. In
more severe cases,
the judicial threat of reversing custody or terminating
access may be the most effective way to end emotionally abusive conduct by an
alienating parent; judicial continuity helps make this a credible threat
.

[
1059
]

Once again, this court finds that case management by one judge to
deal with all motions is appropriate. There is far less likelihood of a court
being manipulated in such instances and a far greater likelihood of consistency,
predictability and stability.

As suggested in this article produced on behalf of the respondent,

K.
Varying Custody

The
most dramatic judicial response to alienation is to transfer custody from the
alienating parent to the rejected parent. If an application is made to vary
custody, the court must first be satisfied that a “material change of
circumstances” occurred since the original custody arrangement was made.
Second, the court must determine that it is in the best interests of the
children. In these cases, it is usually necessary for a parent seeking a
variation in custody to have expert testimony to establish that the child has
been alienated and that any emotional trauma to the child from the change will
be limited in duration. Although the courts are reluctant to vary custody, as
it can be very disruptive to children, in several recent cases,
appellate
courts have affirmed the transfer of custody from an alienating parent. The
courts recognized that a change in custody was the only effective way to end
the emotional harm caused by an alienating custodial parent
.

2.

Active alienators

There are a number of reasons why this court finds that remedy to be

[
1093
]

This court is not prepared
to give up on these children at this point and is not prepared to give up on
the children being able to have a normalized relationship with their mother
(and with their father). The younger children are ten and not yet twelve. The
oldest child has just turned fourteen.

[
1094
]

The court finds that in its
opinion intervention is likely to assist. The court further finds there is no
trauma to any of the children being placed with their mother.

[
1095
]

As
mentioned
elsewhere in this decision, the court finds
that the severance of the relationship between the children and their mother is
in no way due to “justified estrangement”.

[
1096
]

While the parental conflict
that may result from continuing the litigation is never in a child’s best
interest, the court finds that having no relationship or the likelihood of no
relationship
with their
mother is far less in the children’s best interests than the intervention which
is being ordered by this court.

[
1097
]

To the applicant’s credit,
even though undoubtedly she is emotionally and financially
exhausted
, she has
continued with her perseverance to maintain a relationship with these children.
The court finds that this is to her credit and ultimately will be to the
benefit of the children that she has done so.

[
1098
]
