ANALYSIS

[
1100
]

The main issue for this court to decide was whether or not there had
been a material change in circumstances since the order of Justice Corkery in
2013 (and as well relating to financial issues in the order of Justice Wildman
in 2014).

[
1101
]

If the court were to find that there had not been a material change
in circumstances, then the court would not proceed further and the order of
Justice Corkery would remain as it is.

[
1102
]

If, however, the court finds that there has been a material change
in circumstances, then the court must take the second step and determine
whether or not any change in the order is in the best interests of the
children.

[
1103
]

The consent order was largely based on the parenting plan crafted by
Howard Hurwitz after a section 30 custody access assessment.

[
1104
]

Even though that custody access assessment report is now clearly
dated and is four years old, this court finds that it does have significant
probative value to assist the court in determining the issues that are before
it.

[
1105
]

There has been no updated section 30 assessment report and,
therefore, the court is not relying on the assessment nor on any evidence by
Mr. Hurwitz with respect to what is the current situation.

[
1106
]

However, the court notes that at the conclusion of his custody
access assessment report, Mr. Hurwitz expressed some reservation as to what the
future would hold for this family. Unfortunately, his concern was well founded.

[
1107
]

The psychological testing of the parties is something else that this
court finds particularly helpful in analysing what has occurred.

[
1108
]

In addition, the court finds that many of the concerns cited by Mr.
Hurwitz in his section 30 custody access report are concerns that have been
amplified since then.

[
1109
]

The particular issue that this court finds that needs to be decided
is whether or not the material change in circumstances has occurred and whether
or not there has been any alienation by the respondent.

[
1110
]

Both parties agree that the current situation is not in the best
interests of the children.

[
1111
]

Each of the parties, however, has a different solution to the
problem. The respondent would have the court believe that the children have on
their own made a decision that they do not wish to spend 50% of their time with
their mother. He would further have the court believe that the reason for the
children’s decision is because of the mother’s actions and has nothing to do
with any influence that he may have had over the children.

[
1112
]

In fact, his evidence is that he encourages the children to spend
time with their mother.

[
1113
]

The court finds that there are a number of problems with that
hypothesis.

[
1114
]

The court finds that there is absolutely no evidence, save and
except the applicant’s reaction to the actions of the children, to indicate
that the applicant is in any way acting inappropriately towards the children.

[
1115
]

Other than the children’s bald statements that their mother “hits us
all the time” there is not a piece of evidence to indicate that the mother is,
in any way, mistreating the children physically, emotionally or in any other way.

[
1116
]

The applicant has engaged in verbal confrontations with the children
and on the rare occasion has sworn at the children.

[
1117
]

However, on the other hand, there is overwhelming evidence that the
children have physically assaulted their mother on a number of occasions.

[
1118
]

These assaults have included:

•

Jane grabbing her mother by the throat and pushing
her.

•

James punching and hitting his mother.

•

Throwing water bottles at her in the car while
she was driving on Highway 400.

•

Jane throwing her lunch pail at the mother and
striking her in the eye which resulted in Jane being arrested by the officer
who witnessed this.

•

The children climbing all over their mother
while she is driving (or stopped at a stop sign while driving) as shown in the
infamous video.

•

The children jumping on their mother to retrieve
an iPod which the children claim she has no right to take from them because it
is “theirs” even when they are using it inappropriately and as a result being
late for school.

[
1119
]

In addition to the physical assaults by the children on their
mother, the children have used the most vile of language to their mother on
multiple occasions.

[
1120
]

The court has recounted some, but not all, of those in its decision
and sees no need to once again reiterate the vile language used by these children.
Suffice it to say that no child should ever think it is appropriate to use the
type of language used by these children, let alone when using it on their own
mother.

[
1121
]

The court finds it abhorrent that the respondent would, by his
actions, apparently not only not admonish the children for their behaviour but
in some ways through his inaction, and possibly his action, encourage such
behaviour.

[
1122
]

What is even more deeply disturbing is that these are not children
who typically behave in this manner. The respondent prides himself on how well
behaved, well-mannered,  empathetic and polite these children are in every
other circumstance, save and except interactions with their mother.

[
1123
]

The respondent would have the court believe that it is the mother’s
“fault”.

[
1124
]

On the other hand, the applicant takes the position that the
respondent, likely his girlfriend and his extended family have, basically,
partaken in a campaign to alienate the children from their mother. The court
finds that there is a plethora of evidence to substantiate this claim.

[
1125
]

The court finds that the alienation by the respondent started off
probably almost inadvertently and subconsciously (like the naïve alienator
referred to in this decision). The court contrasts the respondent’s position
with that of the applicant, who in the opinion of the court would have ample
reason to blame the respondent for the attitude of the children.  Yet the
applicant acknowledges that some of Jane’s behaviour may be related to “being a
thirteen year old girl”.  Further, the applicant acknowledged the
inappropriateness of some of her own behaviour.

[
1126
]

The court finds that this alienation started when the parties sat
down to tell the children about the separation.

[
1127
]

At that meeting, the court finds that the respondent cried uncontrollably
and clearly sent a message to the children that he was the “victim” in the
mother’s decision to separate. While it may have been emotionally disturbing
for the respondent to deal with the separation, he owed it to his children to
not demonstrate this type of emotion in front of them. The court is not
convinced that he did this deliberately to gain their sympathy, but certainly
the court finds that he could have controlled himself much better.  In his job
as a firefighter and now as an Acting District Chief, undoubtedly, the
respondent is in situations where he must be able to control his emotions.

[
1128
]

The alienation then continued throughout the time of the nesting
agreement. The trivial nature of the respondent posting a note that the
applicant had allegedly “stolen his gum” is an example of the type of nonsense
to which the children were exposed.

[
1129
]

Another example early on that the court found was most telling, was
the fact that the applicant had given the children as a Christmas gift, a
recording of her reading bedtime stories to them. This gift mysteriously
disappeared. The email correspondence reveals that the respondent of course
claims that he had nothing to do with its disappearance.

[
1130
]

The court finds that they were multiple indicia of parental alienation.
As the court has analogized some of those jigsaw pieces were far bigger than
others.

[
1131
]

One of the big pieces of the jigsaw puzzle for this court is that
the children had enjoyed, and were very good, at skiing prior to the
separation. However, following the separation as soon as he could (given John’s
illness immediately following the separation) the respondent ensured that the
children would not be going skiing but would be playing hockey. What better way
to take the children away from an activity that they had enjoyed with their
mother and to put them in an activity which the respondent enjoyed.

[
1132
]

Given their young ages at the time, even if he wanted to put them
into hockey, a reasonable compromise would have been to let the applicant take
them skiing while she had them for weekends and the respondent could take them
to hockey while he had them.

[
1133
]

That, however, did not fit with the respondent’s plans.

[
1134
]

When the court looks at the book that Mr. Hurwitz co-authored
relating to parental alienation (and even the articles to which the respondent
referred the court) and the indicia of severe alienation, it is almost as if
this book was written about the respondent, or if, on the other hand, he read
this book as a guide on “how to alienate”.

[
1135
]

The reaction of the children to C.T. and her family is another huge
red flag for this court when it comes to the alienation piece. Ms. C.T.’s
evidence is that the children enjoyed a good relationship with her, her mother
and her children prior to the separation. When she did see the children
following the separation they were cold to her and did not want to engage with
her. There is no logical explanation for this other than some external
influence on the children to not engage with anyone associated with the
applicant.

[
1136
]

The action of James and John jumping out of the applicant’s van
rather than going for a visit to Ms. C.T.’s house is extreme beyond any
comprehension. There is absolutely no reason why the children would be so
traumatized by going to visit Ms. C.T. that they would take this action. The
respondent’s explanation is shallow at best that they were upset that they were
not going to be with their teammates at a meal at a hockey tournament.

[
1137
]

In Mr. Hurwitz’s section 30 report, he comments on the respondent
saying that he needed to speak to the children three times a day, a comment
which the respondent denies having made.

[
1138
]

The court finds that another big piece in the alienation puzzle is
the respondent’s obsessive calls to the children or the children’s obsessive
calls to the respondent and his girlfriend.

[
1139
]

The applicant’s evidence is that each morning the children call
their father a number of times and as a result are late getting up and getting
ready for school. The respondent denies this. However, the children, in their discussions
with the counsellor, virtually tell the same story as does the applicant. They
admit to speaking with their father in the morning. James says he talks to him
at least twice.

[
1140
]

There is absolutely no reason for the respondent to have to speak to
the children this frequently while their mother is attempting to get them ready
for school. The applicant is not mistreating the children.

She in fact
is making them a nutritious breakfast which the children sometimes do not get
to enjoy because they are spending the time on the phone with the respondent or
his girlfriend.

[
1141
]

There is no reason for the respondent to be doing this other than to
deliberately attempt to sabotage the children’s relationship with their mother
and to frustrate the applicant.

[
1142
]

The nighttime routine with the children is the same. The children
are on the phone with the respondent or his girlfriend far later than children
of that age should be up. The applicant’s evidence, which is accepted by this
court, is that quite often on a school night Jane will be on the phone with her
father or his girlfriend until past midnight or sometimes one o’clock in the
morning. It is little wonder that she is not able to get up for school the next
morning when she needs to be up at 7:15 a.m.

[
1143
]

The same thing occurs with James who is also up late on the phone
with his father or the father’s girlfriend.

[
1144
]

John as well is on the phone with his father or his father’s
girlfriend far later than a child of that age should be up on a school night.

[
1145
]

This court finds that the frequency of calls by the respondent to
the children or by the children to the respondent while they are with their
mother, is clear indicia in this case of alienation attempts by the father. It
is consistent with what is set out in Mr. Hurwitz’s book. As well, it is
consistent with what Mr. Hurwitz put in his assessment report now four years
ago and what he testified at trial. At that time, the respondent was insisting
on calling the children at least three times per day while they were at their
mother’s. Mr. Hurwitz in his testimony indicated that that was a clear red flag
for him. This court finds that it is a huge red flag for it. There is, in the
opinion of this court, no logical explanation for such frequent phone calls by
the father to the children or him encouraging the children to call him other
than to create problems between the children and their mother and to interfere
with the mother’s attempts at parenting the children while they are with her.

[
1146
]

Another huge piece of the puzzle when it comes to alienation is the
fortuitous event when the applicant’s text messages began going to Jane’s iPod.
The respondent claims that he and his girlfriend were fearful that the
applicant was threatening harm particularly to the girlfriend. This court does
not believe for a second that the respondent took seriously those “threats”; in
fact, even the respondent admitted that he, within a short period of time,
realized that the applicant was only venting.

[
1147
]

However, this court finds that the respondent jumped on the
opportunity to take advantage of this situation. Firstly, he immediately had Jane
send him a screenshot so that he could take it to the police. Notwithstanding
his protestations to the contrary, this court finds that he had every intention
of having the applicant charged and that he was, in fact, upset when she was
not charged. The Society records virtually say as much based on the
respondent’s own comments to the Society.

[
1148
]

To make matters even worse, however, the respondent then felt it was
appropriate to have a twelve year old daughter surreptitiously spying on her
mother for a period of six weeks while he gathered evidence against the mother.

[
1149
]

The respondent then has the audacity to claim that the daughter was
traumatized by some of the messages that she saw between the applicant and her
then boyfriend.

[
1150
]

Of course the respondent totally ignores the fact that Jane would
not have been exposed to any of these messages if, upon discovering what was
occurring, he had picked up the phone and told the applicant what was
happening.

[
1151
]

In mid-December 2015 and again in January 2016 the respondent is
telling the Society not to alert the applicant to the fact of that he, his
girlfriend and the twelve year old daughter (and likely James and possibly John)
are reading these messages tells the whole story.

[
1152
]

This court found that the applicant’s evidence was forthright and
has no issues with her credibility.

[
1153
]

On the other hand, the respondent’s evidence was what the court
would call “polished”. He was slick and had an answer (albeit in this court’s
opinion implausible in virtually every instance) for any allegation made
against him.

[
1154
]

The issue with the sporting equipment is another piece of the
alienation puzzle. The respondent puts in place a no trespass order so that the
applicant cannot come on his property to pick up the children’s sporting
equipment, including their bulky hockey bags and baseball equipment. Instead,
there is an absolutely ridiculous situation whereby the applicant has to wait
on the shoulder of the road at the end of the respondent’s 200 foot driveway
while the children (and sometimes the respondent in his truck) bring out their
equipment.

[
1155
]

The situation is exacerbated because the children do not simply go
in and get their equipment but, they then have to spend fifteen or more minutes
talking to the respondent or his girlfriend, or doing whatever, while the
applicant “patiently waits”.

[
1156
]

The court finds that this is just another action by the respondent
to frustrate, hurt and undermine the applicant.

[
1157
]

Instead of simply allowing the children to take their equipment to
the applicant’s residence while they are with her for seven days, the
respondent insists that it be at his home. Just another piece of the alienation
puzzle that the court has found.

[
1158
]

The issue of the respondent’s girlfriend calling the police to
allege that she was concerned the house had been broken into when the children
had attended to pick up their equipment in her absence is simply another
example. It resulted in the applicant, not surprisingly, insisting on having
email confirmation from the respondent prior to going with the children to pick
up the equipment. Had she not done so, one can only speculate as to what other
allegations would have been made against her.

[
1159
]

The children find this very frustrating. That comes as absolutely no
surprise to this court.

[
1160
]

However, the children see this as “their mother’s fault”.

[
1161
]

The views and preferences report and the notes made by Alyssa
Koenderink are very enlightening to this court.

[
1162
]

In addition to that which the court has already mentioned about the
telephone calls to the father while with the mother, there are other pieces
that tell a very clear story.

[
1163
]

While the children have to be prodded multiple times by their mother
to get up in the morning for school, at their father’s, they immediately get up
and enjoy breakfast together.

[
1164
]

When the applicant on a day off suggests to her daughter that they
shoot hoops together, the daughter does not wish to do so but by contrast
enjoys time together with her father and his girlfriend.

[
1165
]

The court finds that this is not because the applicant is someone
with whom Jane does not wish to spend time but is, as a result of the
respondent’s multiple actions, a chronic pattern to undermine the relationship
between these children and their mother.

[
1166
]

When asked, the children could not find anything wrong with their
father while they virtually cannot find anything right with their mother. That
is another very big indication of severe parental alienation.

[
1167
]

In the charts demonstrating indicators of severe alienation, it is
shown that in the end, the alienating parent even “encourages” the children to
spend time with the alienated parent. The respondent claims that he does so.

[
1168
]

The respondent undoubtedly felt that he had “a smoking gun” when he
received the video from Jane relating to the applicant’s driving.

[
1169
]

As was stated by this court earlier in this decision, this court in
no way condones the applicant holding an electronic device and deleting
messages from it while driving.

[
1170
]

On the other hand, this court finds it abhorrent that a father could
watch this video of his children treating their mother in such a manner and not
find it repugnant and worthy of some major correction.  It would not be a
stretch of the imagination that the respondent would encourage and condone his
children recording this type of action. The circumstances that led to that
action are, in this court’s opinion, a culmination of frustration by the
applicant to the total mistreatment that she had been receiving from the
children.

[
1171
]

The respondent cannot claim that he had no idea of what he was
doing. This court finds the transcript of the two attendances by the respondent
before Justice Graham to be another big piece of this alienation puzzle.

[
1172
]

Justice Graham makes it crystal clear to the respondent that the
applicant is not seeking police enforcement because she wants her children in
the back of a police cruiser.

[
1173
]

Justice Graham made it crystal clear that the applicant was seeking
police enforcement in order to motivate the respondent to do that which Justice
Graham implored him to do and that was, to encourage the children and ensure
that they went for their visitation time with their mother.

[
1174
]

In fact, Justice Graham said directly to the respondent “who’s fault
will it be if the police have to enforce this order” and the respondent
somewhat reluctantly acknowledged that it would be his fault.

[
1175
]

The evidence shows that over the last two years since that
appearance in July 2015, rather than encouraging the children to go to their
mother’s, the respondent has done anything but. The result has been that the
police have enforced the visitation order and the children have been exposed to
the trauma of being put in a police cruiser to be taken to visit their mother.

[
1176
]

As did Justice Graham, this court finds the blame for the enforcement
being necessary clearly lies at the feet of the respondent, not the applicant.

[
1177
]

The respondent believes that this has had the desired effect because
the children resent strongly the police enforcement clause. They view this as
“their mother’s fault”. This court is certain that while the respondent may
well have shared many other court documents with the children, he has not
shared the transcript of Justice Graham’s interaction with him wherein Justice
Graham points out and he acknowledges that if police enforcement is required it
is his fault.

[
1178
]

The respondent takes issue with Mr. Hurwitz. He claims that Mr.
Hurwitz was not neutral and did not give him an ample opportunity to respond
and that the assessor did not take into account all of his issues. He claims
that he had problems with Mr. Hurwitz’s “process”.

[
1179
]

The court has read the assessment report and heard all of the
evidence. The court does not find any fault with the assessment report nor with
the process engaged by the assessor.

[
1180
]

The court notes that the parenting plan crafted by the assessor was
essentially the plan that was adopted by the parties in a consent order almost
immediately thereafter. The respondent did not at the time file any objection
to the section 30 assessment because there was no reason to do so.

[
1181
]

The respondent also takes issue with the parenting coordinator Mr. Manning.

[
1182
]

The respondent takes issue with Doug Cochrane of the Society.

[
1183
]

The respondent takes issue with the OPP officers who in their notes
after 30 plus occurrence reports, indicate that they believe that the
respondent is influencing these children. They also indicate that the language
used by the children is not typical language used by children but is, in their
opinions, indicative of having been coached.

[
1184
]

The respondent takes issue with the TLC report.

[
1185
]

This court finds that the respondent takes issue with anyone and
anything which is not in accordance with the respondent’s view of the world.

[
1186
]

This court notes in the psychological assessment done by Dr. Olga
Henderson of the respondent as part of the assessment process, she mentioned
multiple times that the respondent has a need “to be in control”.

[
1187
]

While this may be an admirable quality for someone aspiring to be a
fire chief, it is not a quality that is helpful in a healthy marriage or in
raising children in a healthy manner.

[
1188
]

In conclusion, this court to use the analogy of a jigsaw puzzle
finds that all of the pieces fit together to create a high definition picture
of severe parental alienation by the respondent.

CONCLUSION

[
1189
]

There are four particular actions that, to this court, demonstrate
the character and intent of the respondent.

Ladies Ski Day

[
1190
]

There was much evidence about the respondent texting the applicant
on this day but that is not the real issue.

[
1191
]

There was a great deal of evidence about Ladies Ski Day and the
respondent’s reaction to the applicant taking a day off from work to go skiing
with her friends.
Basically,
his own evidence
is that the objection that he had to that was that she was taking a day off
work, essentially cheating her employer by stealing time from her employer and
that she was using that time in a public place where she might “get caught”. He
indicated that based on his work through the Firefighters Association he knew
that this type of action was something that could result in justifiable
termination from employment.

[
1192
]

However, he testified that he really did not have a problem if she
took a day off work to spend it at home with him (or the children). His
rationale was that she was not in a public place and therefore was highly
unlikely to “get caught”.

[
1193
]

This demonstrates the respondent’s character which is further
demonstrated through actions after the separation. The message is it is okay to
cheat as long as you do so in a manner in which you are not likely to get
caught.

Inadvertent Interception of Text Message

[
1194
]

The second extremely telling action by the respondent is in relation
to Jane inadvertently receiving the applicant’s text messages. As I indicated
on the
voir dire
and as this court has indicated in this decision, this
court does not take issue with the fact that the respondent saw the initial
messages, which he viewed as threatening to him and his girlfriend, and asked Jane
to forward copies to him and then brought those copies to the police. Even if
the respondent and his girlfriend were not really fearful that the applicant
would carry out those threats, it is not unreasonable, particularly for someone
in a high conflict separation to utilize that evidence which had fortuitously
fallen into his lap to his benefit, to try to have the applicant charged and
thereby help his custody case.

[
1195
]

What he does next, however, is what this court finds to be very
revealing about his true character. He engages his then twelve year old
daughter as a “spy” to surreptitiously continue to receive these text messages
from her mother’s phone. His own words are the most telling. The reason he did
so and kept the iPod was “to gain evidence”. He gave absolutely no thought to
the fact that this was an invasion of the applicant’s privacy. He further gave
no thought to the fact that he was teaching modelling and encouraging a twelve
year old child not only to spy on her mother but to lie to her mother. This
court has absolutely no doubt that he knew that in January 2016 the applicant
was questioning Jane as to the whereabouts of her iPod and that he probably was
encouraging his twelve year old daughter, or if not encouraging, at least
acquiescing to her lying to her mother.

[
1196
]

This is tantamount to being so desirous of taking out the applicant
that he was not the least bit concerned that by doing so he was thrusting the
bayonet through his child to get to the applicant.

Frequent Telephone Calls

[
1197
]

Another example is the chronic telephone by the respondent. He
insists on talking to the children multiple times each day including so doing
on school mornings. He is doing so in this court’s view in a deliberate attempt
to sabotage any relationship that the applicant has with the children. He does
so knowing that it will cause conflict between the children and their mother.
He is totally oblivious to the fact that this is causing the children to be
late for school. His sole motivation is to “get the applicant”.

[
1198
]

His late night telephone calls to the children or even from the
children, are identical. His sole motivation again is to cause problems between
the applicant and the children. He goes out of his way to undermine her
authority by telling the children that the electronic devices are “theirs” and
that if their mother tries to take them away it is “stealing”. At one point he
tells the children to call the police if she does so. Once again, the messaging
is abhorrent. For someone who is an Acting District Chief and presumably
aspiring to be a chief of a major fire department, it is appalling to this
court that he would find this type of behaviour acceptable and that he with his
own children would encourage and model behaviour that is a deliberate attempt
to undermine authority, in this case the authority of his children’s mother.

Taylor Swift Concert

[
1199
]

Of all that he has done perhaps the lowest of his actions is the
Taylor Swift concert.  For Jane’s twelfth birthday the applicant had bought
them Taylor Swift tickets for a concert that fall.  The applicant had made
arrangements for she and Jane to go with another friend and her mother.  Jane
was ecstatic.  The concert, however, was to take place on the respondent’s
“time”.  Being thusly “in control” he bought floor level tickets so that he (or
his designate) could take Jane thus depriving the applicant and Jane of time
together.

[
1200
]

To quote Philip Epstein as I did elsewhere, alienation is something
that “you know it when you see it”.  The Taylor Swift concert incident shows
severe alienation in 3D, High Definition, or 4K.  The respondent could not have
made the severe alienation more crystal clear than that.

[
1201
]

To use a word picture that the respondent as a firefighter may
understand, it is as if the respondent has climbed up the ladder (as he is done
in his career quite successfully) and got to the top but unfortunately his
ladder has been against the wrong wall. This court finds that his motivation
from the time that the applicant had the audacity to tell him that she was
separating is to, as the applicant claimed, declare war against her and take
the children from her. His view of success at the top of the ladder was to
create a situation whereby the applicant was marginalized from the children’s
lives.

[
1202
]

It was very telling that Jane stated “I don’t need my mother because
I have C.A..” The respondent, undoubtedly, believes that that is the case.
Throughout his evidence he consistently used “we” referring to he and C.A. in
reference to the children. He even started out by saying that we (referring to
himself and C.A.) have three children. The unfortunate part for the respondent
is that he does not realize that a healthy relationship with their mother is
something that benefits the three children. He also does not appreciate that
not having a healthy relationship with a parent is something pursuant to which
countless studies show, has a very detrimental effect on children as adults
with their relationships with others, with drug abuse, alcohol abuse and
various other problems.

[
1203
]

For the respondent, one can only hope that he will realize while at
the top of this ladder that the wall that he should have been climbing is one
in which the children have a healthy relationship with both parents. They can
also have love for C.A.. The fact that a child has love for an additional
person does not mean that they need to have less love for their biological
parents. Love is not a finite vessel in which, if you give love to someone you
have to take it away from someone else.

[
1204
]

This court has absolutely no doubt about what needs to be done in
order to attempt to restore a relationship between the children and their
mother.

[
1205
]

For that reason, this court will be ordering the Family Bridges
program as a restorative measure of the relationship between the children and
their mother.

[
1206
]

In order for this restoration to have any chance of success, there
also needs to be a period of time when the children have no contact with the
respondent, the respondent’s girlfriend, the respondent’s parents, and the
respondent’s brother.

[
1207
]

The recommended period of time is a minimum of ninety days.

[
1208
]

It will be for the respondent and the children to determine if the
timeframe needs to be longer than that.

[
1209
]

If the children and the respondent embrace the therapy that is
available to them, then the timeframe may not need to be longer than 90 days.
If, however, the respondent and the children decide to fight this process and,
in the case of the respondent, not accept responsibility for his actions, then
the timeframe will undoubtedly have to be longer, perhaps much longer with
supervised access.

[
1210
]

This court will also take on a role of case managing through future
motions so that all future motions until otherwise ordered by this court will
come before it. This court has had the opportunity to hear fourteen days of
evidence in this matter and views itself as the most appropriate forum to
monitor this family moving forward.

[
1211
]

At risk of being accused of being the ultimate optimist, this court
believes that there is no reason why, if the children and the respondent and his
extended family engage positively and embrace the therapy available, that a
situation which involved 30 plus police occurrences, multiple open Society
files, a custody access assessment, a parenting coordinator, therapy for the
children, and at least  sixteen court orders and endorsements, including this
one, cannot in the future become a situation whereby the police, the Society
and other professionals need not be involved because these children have a
healthy relationship with both parents which is supported by both parents.

ORDER

[
1212
]

For all of the reasons set out above, this court orders the
following:

1.

The Orders of Corkery
J. dated November 15, 2013 and Wildman J. dated April 28, 2014 are varied by
the terms of this Order as set out herein.

2.

The applicant shall
have sole temporary custody of the children Jane date of birth […], 2003, James
born […], 2005 John born […], 2007 (hereinafter “Jane, James and John and/or
collectively “the children”).

3.

The applicant shall
not be required until further order of this court to consult with or seek the
respondent’s input with respect to any decisions to be made on behalf of the
children.

4.

The children shall be
in the residential care of the applicant pending further order of this Court.

5.

The applicant shall enroll
with the children in FAMILY BRIDGES: A WORK SHOP FOR TROUBLED AND ALIENATED
PARENT-CHILD RELATION SHIPS (Family Bridges), to enable and assist the children
in adjusting to living with the applicant.

6.

Following the
completion of the Family Bridges workshop, and before returning home with the
children, the applicant shall take the children on a vacation of no less than 5
days in duration.  The Court expects that the children will apply what they
learn during the Family Bridges workshop to improve their interactions with
their mother during and following their vacation.

7.

The applicant has the
right to conceal from the respondent the location of any intervention sought
for the children (e.g., educational or mental health intervention) in the
interests of protecting the children and the intervention from intrusion,
interruption, and harassment.

8.

Based on earlier
direction given by this Court, the children are present at court and the
respondent is to leave the courthouse directly after meeting with the children
at the instance of this Court today and until further Order of this Court is
not to be within 500 metres of the children commencing immediately after
transfer;

9.

The respondent is to
ensure the children's belongings are delivered by a third-party to the applicant’s
home within 10 days, at the respondent’s expense. For greater clarity,
“belongings” shall include:

(a)

the children’s birth
certificates;

(b)

the children’s passports;

(c)

the children’s health cards;

(d)

the children’s report cards;

(e)

the children’s hockey and
baseball equipment;

(f)

all of the children’s
electronic devices in the possession or control of the respondent including but
not limited to iPhones, iPads, iPods and any other electronic devices in his
possession or control.

10.

The applicant has the
sole authority to consent to the children's travel. Until further order of this
Court, any requirement that the respondent consent to travel for the children
outside Canada is hereby dispensed with. Further, should the children’s
passports need to be renewed prior to further order of this Court, the
respondent’s consent to the renewal of the children’s passports is hereby
dispensed with.

11.

The respondent will
sign any consents to release information to the applicant or Family Bridges, as
required by the intervention/treatment professionals, and within 24 hours of
any such request being presented to him by the applicant or by the
intervention/treatment professionals. Should his consent not be delivered
within 24 hours of any such request, then his consent is hereby dispensed with
and any doctors, dentists, schools, school boards or other professionals shall
release the information requested with respect to the children on the sole
consent of the applicant.

12.

A copy of the Section
30 Custody Access Assessment report of Howard Hurwitz, all reports from Family
TLC, Alyssa Koenderink, Wendy Hunder, the Society, the police including OPP,
Barrie Police Service and York Regional Police, the Reasons for Decision in
this proceeding and all other relevant information will be provided to any
professional whom the applicant engages to assist with the children, including
Family Bridges team leaders. Any necessity for the respondent’s consent to any
such release is hereby dispensed with.

13.

Since it is in the
children’s best interests, until further Order of this Court the children shall
have no contact with the respondent, his relatives, friends, and associates of
the respondent, including C.A., and the paternal grandparents namely C.2, M., the
paternal uncle C. his spouse or children whose influence is likely to interfere
with the children's progress in effectively repairing the damaged relationship
with the applicant, except as directed by Family Bridges, or the aftercare
professional, or any other professional designated by the applicant or the
Court; and none of the aforementioned individuals shall have any contact with
the children.

14.

"Contact"
includes all forms of contact (direct or indirect) and communication, including
but not limited to phone contact, text messages, letters, emails, contact
through social media or other contact via computer, in-person contact, and
communication via third parties;

15.

The duration of the
no-contact order shall be determined by the Court, but shall be no less than 90
days from return of the children to the home of the applicant, or other
designated post Family Bridges residence after the successful completion of the
structured Family Bridges Workshop and the post Workshop vacation period;

16.

The Court will determine
the conditions, timing and nature of resumption of contact between the children
and respondent with the assistance and input from the Aftercare Specialist;

17.

The resumption, timing
and nature of contact between the children and respondent will be based on the
cooperation of the children and respondent with these Orders, with the Family
Bridges program, and with the Aftercare specialist;

18.

The applicant has the
authority to confiscate and prevent the children's use of cell phones, iPads,
iPods, pagers, blackberries, and computers even if the respondent provides such
equipment;

19.

During the no-contact
period, the respondent and each of those individuals named in paragraph 13
hereof, shall stay at least 500 metres away from the applicant and the
children, their residence, their vehicle, and the children's schools or other
places frequented by the children; including any sports venues where the
children are participating. The applicant shall advise the respondent by email,
text or Our Family Wizard in the event that the children will be in attendance
at any such venues. It is the respondent’s responsibility to ensure that this
is communicated to those other individuals named in paragraph 13 hereof.

20.

The applicant and the
respondent shall within 10 days of the date of this Order set up communication

that software program.

21.

All communication
between the parties shall be though OFW thereafter, except in emergency

whereupon unless mutually agreed, future communication shall be through OFW.

22.

In accordance with s.
36(2) of the
Children’s Law Reform Act
, any police services in Ontario,
including the Barrie Police Service, the Ontario Provincial Police, the York

[…], 2005 and John born […], 2007 to the applicant in accordance with this
Order and may enter upon any premises, place or location at any time for the

23.

The applicant shall
have possession and control of the children's passports and birth certificates,

24.

Neither party shall
subpoena the records of any of the professionals who assist the applicant and

team leaders from communication with aftercare specialists and any
professionals.

25.

If the applicant
elects to participate with the children in Family Bridges, the applicant shall

26.

The respondent shall
reimburse the applicant 100% of the amount paid by the applicant to Family

to Family Bridges. This reimbursement shall constitute a section 7 expense and
shall be collected by the Family Responsibility Office on behalf of the
applicant if not paid by the respondent to her within 5 days of the said
notice.

27.

Neither party will
come to the office of a Family Bridges team leader unless for prescheduled
appointments, nor approach the Family Bridges team leaders at any time in
public, nor phone excessively, nor send threatening communications.

28.

Any violation of any
of the foregoing terms of this Order shall be deemed by this Court to
constitute contempt of court and shall be subject to, upon motion before this
Court, the sanctions provided in the
Family Law Rules
for contempt of
court which shall include fines and or imprisonment.

29.

The respondent shall
pay to the applicant arrears of child support in the amount of $6,734.00 representing

2014 for the months of May 2015 to and including June 2017. This amount shall
be paid within 7 days of the date of this order failing which the said amount
shall be collected by the Family Responsibility Office.

30.

Commencing July 1,
2017 and on the 1
st
day of each month thereafter until further order
of this Court, the respondent shall pay child support to the applicant for the
3 children in the amount of $2,521.00 per month based on the respondent’s
disclosed income for 2016 in the amount of $143,897.00.

31.

The parties shall
submit costs submissions, not exceeding 4 pages in length each, not including
any bills of costs or offers to settle. The applicant’s cost submissions shall
be served and filed by no later than July 31, 2017, the respondent’s responding
submissions by no later than August 15, 2017 and the applicant’s reply
submissions, if any, by August 31, 2017. All cost submissions shall be filed in
the Continuing Record and in addition to filing the same shall be forwarded by
email to the attention of this Court’s Judicial Assistant.

32.

Until further order of
this Court, any future motions to be brought by either party shall be heard by
this Court.

33.

This matter is
adjourned it to a motion before this Court as noted in the signed Order. The

Each party shall file a 14C no later than 2:00 p.m. two days prior to the
return of this motion.

34.

Upon the return of
this matter, this Court will make a determination as to any changes that are to
be made to the noncontact order with the respondent. The noncontact order with
the respondent shall not be varied until a minimum of 75 days have passed from
the commencement of therapy recommended by Family Bridges for the respondent.
This 75 day period is a minimum only, the extension of which will be considered
by this Court based on the respondent’s progress made in any therapeutic
program recommended by Family Bridges.  This Court will consider the following
prior to ordering resumption of contact between the respondent and the
children:

(a)

the degree of compliance by the respondent with
the requirement of the Family Bridges program;

(b)

the degree to which the respondent has promoted
the children’s relationship with the applicant;

(c)

the degree to which the respondent’s behaviours
and comments are congruent with the promotion of a positive relationship
between the children and the applicant;

(d)

after the respondent has resumed contact with
the children, whether or not the respondent has been critical of the applicant;

(e)

such other criteria as recommended by the Family
Bridges program.

35.

Support Deduction
Order to issue.

36.

This Order bears
post-judgment interest at the rate of 2% per annum effective from the date of
this Order.  Where there is a default in payment, the payment in default
shall bear interest only from the date of default.

37.

Unless this Order is
withdrawn from the Director’s Office, Family Responsibility Office, it shall be

Director, who shall pay them to the person to whom they are owed.

38.

For as long as child
support is to be paid, the payor and recipient, if applicable must provide

Child
Support Guidelines.
